os-filesystems-io:5.body:
## Two separate questions
1. Does the call wait? (blocking vs non-blocking)
2. Who does the work after the call returns? (synchronous vs asynchronous)

## Blocking I/O
read() puts the thread to sleep until data arrives; simple; needs a thread per concurrent operation.

## Non-blocking I/O
Set O_NONBLOCK. If data is not ready, read() returns immediately with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK. You must retry; polling in a loop wastes CPU.

## I/O multiplexing (readiness notification)
select/poll/epoll/kqueue tell you when an fd is ready, then you call read/write (non-blocking), which copies the data synchronously. One thread handles thousands of connections. This is what Node, nginx, Redis and Netty use. The copy still happens in your thread, and regular files are always reported ready (so disk reads still block; libuv uses a thread pool).

## True asynchronous I/O
You submit the operation, the kernel does it (including the copy) and notifies you on completion. Examples: Windows IOCP, Linux io_uring (shared submission and completion rings; supports files and sockets, batches syscalls), older Linux AIO (limited to O_DIRECT).

## Comparison
- Blocking: simplest; thread-per-connection; cost: memory and context switches.
- Non-blocking + readiness (reactor pattern): high concurrency, callback or state-machine code; you do the I/O when notified.
- Async completion (proactor pattern): the kernel does the I/O and delivers results; fewest syscalls, more complex ownership of buffers.
- Do not confuse with a language async/await: that is syntax over one of the above.

## Worked example
Web server with 10,000 mostly idle clients:
- Blocking threads: 10,000 threads, ~10,000 stacks and scheduler entries.
- epoll loop: one thread, epoll_wait returns the ~50 ready sockets, each handled by a non-blocking read and write.
- io_uring: submit batches of reads and sends in one syscall and harvest completions; reduces syscall overhead at very high QPS (hundreds of thousands to millions of ops/s).

## Pitfalls
- Partial reads and writes: non-blocking write may accept fewer bytes; keep an output buffer and wait for writable.
- Edge-triggered epoll: read until EAGAIN.
- Blocking calls hidden in handlers (DNS, disk, a CPU-heavy loop) stall the loop.
- Back-pressure: stop reading when the writer cannot keep up.

## Follow-ups
- Is epoll asynchronous I/O? No: it is readiness notification, synchronous I/O multiplexing.
- POSIX terms: blocking, non-blocking, I/O multiplexing, signal-driven, asynchronous are the five models from Stevens.
keyPoints: Blocking and non-blocking describe whether the call waits; sync and async describe who completes the transfer.
epoll/kqueue are readiness-based multiplexing (reactor); IOCP and io_uring are completion-based (proactor).
Regular files are always 'ready', so disk I/O needs a thread pool or io_uring.
Handle partial reads/writes and never block inside the event loop.

os-filesystems-io:6.body:
## Two ways to read a file
- read/write: the kernel copies data from the page cache into your buffer (and back for writes). One syscall per call; two copies in total (disk to page cache by DMA, page cache to user buffer).
- mmap: maps the file's pages into your address space. Access with ordinary loads and stores; the first touch causes a page fault that maps the cached page. No copy into a user buffer, no per-access syscall.

## mmap details
```c
int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDONLY);
char *p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
x = p[offset];          // may page-fault, no read() call
munmap(p, len);
```
- MAP_SHARED: writes go to the file (via the page cache, flushed lazily, msync to force). MAP_PRIVATE: copy-on-write, changes are not written back.
- Anonymous mmap (MAP_ANONYMOUS) is how malloc gets large blocks.
- Shared libraries and executables are mmap'd; processes share the same physical pages.
- Shared memory IPC: two processes map the same file or shm object.

## When mmap wins
- Random access to large read-mostly files (index files, embedded databases like LMDB), many processes sharing the same data, zero-copy-ish access, simple code with pointer arithmetic.

## When read/write wins
- Sequential streaming: read-ahead works well and avoids page-fault overhead; a large read() into a reusable buffer is often as fast or faster.
- Small files: mmap setup and teardown (page table updates, TLB shootdowns) cost more than a single read.
- Need for error handling: I/O errors on mmap arrive as SIGBUS rather than an error return; a truncated file under your mapping crashes you.
- Writes needing durability ordering: with mmap you have less control over when pages hit disk (msync), and databases like PostgreSQL and (recently) others avoid mmap for their buffer pools for this reason, while LMDB embraces it.
- 32-bit address space limits file size mapped.

## Numbers
A page fault for a cached page (minor fault) is about 0.1-1 us; a read() syscall is about 0.1-0.5 us plus copy (about 10 GB/s memcpy, so a 4 KiB copy is roughly 0.4 us). They are comparable per page; the difference shows in access patterns and concurrency (mmap adds mmap_lock contention in multithreaded processes).

## Follow-ups
- Does mmap avoid I/O? No; it avoids the copy and syscall per access. The disk is still read on a miss.
- sendfile/splice: zero-copy from file to socket without bringing data to user space (static file servers).
keyPoints: read/write copies data between page cache and a user buffer; mmap maps cache pages directly into the address space.
mmap suits random access to large read-mostly files and shared data; read suits sequential streaming and small files.
mmap I/O errors and truncation show up as SIGBUS, and durability timing needs msync.
sendfile and splice give zero-copy file-to-socket transfer.

os-security-basics:0.body:
## Why two modes
If any program could execute any instruction or touch any memory, one bug would take down the machine. CPUs provide privilege levels: user mode (ring 3 on x86) restricts instructions and memory access; kernel mode (ring 0) can do everything: program the MMU, talk to devices, disable interrupts, halt the CPU.

## What user mode cannot do
- Execute privileged instructions (load page-table base, I/O port access, HLT, change interrupt state); doing so raises a fault and the kernel kills the process.
- Access kernel memory (page table marks it supervisor-only).
- Access other processes' memory (separate page tables).

## System calls: the controlled gate
To do anything privileged (read a file, send a packet, allocate pages) a program asks the kernel.
1. User code puts the syscall number and arguments in registers (x86-64 Linux: number in rax, args in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9) and executes the syscall instruction. (Usually via libc wrappers like read().)
2. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point set up by the kernel (not a user-chosen address).
3. Kernel validates arguments (pointer ranges, permissions, fd validity), does the work, and puts the result in rax.
4. sysret/iret returns to user mode.
Errors return -errno (libc turns that into -1 plus errno).

## Cost
A syscall is much cheaper than a context switch but not free: ~100-300 ns for a trivial call, more with Spectre/Meltdown mitigations (KPTI swaps page tables). Hence batching: buffered I/O, readv/writev, io_uring, vDSO (gettimeofday and clock_gettime run in user space reading kernel-maintained data without trapping).

## Other transitions into the kernel
- Interrupts (timer, NIC, disk): asynchronous, from hardware.
- Exceptions/faults: page fault, divide by zero, invalid opcode: synchronous, caused by the running instruction.
- Syscalls: deliberate, via a trap.

## Worked example: read(fd, buf, 4096)
User-mode libc wrapper -> syscall instruction -> kernel checks fd and that buf is a writable user range -> page cache lookup (copy_to_user) or block and schedule another process -> returns bytes read.

## Follow-ups
- Why must the kernel validate user pointers? A malicious pointer to kernel memory could read or overwrite it (confused deputy).
- Library vs system call: printf is a library function that eventually calls write.
- Microkernel vs monolithic: microkernels keep less code in ring 0 at the cost of more IPC; Linux is monolithic (modules).
- Container processes still make syscalls to the shared host kernel; that is why seccomp filters matter.
keyPoints: User mode is restricted; the only way to privileged services is a syscall into a kernel-defined entry point.
The kernel validates every argument and pointer from user space.
A syscall costs on the order of 100-300 ns, so batch with buffered I/O, writev or io_uring; vDSO avoids the trap for time calls.
Interrupts, exceptions and syscalls are the three ways control enters the kernel.

os-security-basics:1.body:
## Access control question
Who may do what to which object (file, socket, process)? Two big families.

## DAC: discretionary access control
The owner of an object decides who can access it. Classic Unix permissions:
- Each file has owner, group and mode bits: rwx for user, group, others. Example 0640: owner read/write, group read, others nothing.
- Kernel checks the process's effective uid/gid against the file's mode. uid 0 (root) bypasses most checks.
- ACLs (setfacl) add per-user and per-group entries.
- Weakness: the owner (or any program running with that owner's rights, including malware or an exploited process) can grant access freely, and root is all-powerful: compromise of a setuid or root daemon means total compromise.

## MAC: mandatory access control
A system-wide policy, set by an administrator and enforced by the kernel regardless of ownership; users and even root-owned processes cannot override it.
- SELinux: every process and object gets a label (type); policy rules say which types may do which operations (httpd_t may read httpd_sys_content_t, but not user home files). Default deny. Used on RHEL/Fedora, Android.
- AppArmor: path-based profiles per program (Ubuntu, SUSE).
- Multi-level security (Bell-LaPadula): no read up, no write down, labels like Confidential or Secret.

## Example
A web server is exploited and the attacker has a shell as www-data.
- DAC only: attacker can read anything www-data or world can read (including /etc/passwd, other apps' config if mode 644) and may escalate.
- MAC (SELinux): the process runs in httpd_t; the policy denies reading ssh keys or connecting to unrelated ports even though the file modes would allow it. Damage is confined.

## Related mechanisms
- Linux capabilities split root's power into pieces (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_SYS_ADMIN) so a process can bind port 80 without being root.
- setuid binaries run with the owner's privileges: powerful and risky (passwd, sudo).
- Role-based access control (RBAC) at application level, ABAC (attribute-based) for policies.

## Trade-offs
- DAC: simple and flexible, easy for users; weak against compromised programs.
- MAC: strong containment; complex policy authoring, breakage when policy is too strict (permissive mode, audit2allow to tune).

## Follow-ups
- Why do containers on Docker use SELinux/AppArmor profiles by default (on supporting distributions)? To confine a breakout to the container's label.
- Confused deputy: a privileged program tricked into using its authority for an attacker.
keyPoints: DAC lets owners grant access (Unix mode bits, ACLs); MAC enforces an admin policy that even owners and root-owned processes cannot override.
SELinux uses type labels with default deny; AppArmor uses per-program path profiles.
MAC contains a compromised service; DAC alone does not.
Linux capabilities split root into narrower privileges.

os-security-basics:2.body:
## The bug
Writing more data into a fixed-size buffer than it holds overwrites adjacent memory. On the stack, adjacent memory includes the saved frame pointer and the return address.

## Stack frame (x86-64, simplified, stack grows down)
```
higher addresses
  [ caller frame ...        ]
  [ return address          ]   <- overwritten by attacker
  [ saved rbp               ]
  [ char buf[64]            ]   <- strcpy writes here, upward
lower addresses
```

```c
void greet(char *name) {
    char buf[64];
    strcpy(buf, name);     // no length check
}
```
If name is 100 bytes, bytes 72-79 (after 64 buffer + 8 saved rbp) overwrite the return address. When greet returns, the CPU jumps to the attacker-chosen address.

## Stack smashing classic
Attacker puts shellcode in the buffer and sets the return address to the buffer's address, so execution lands in the injected code (Aleph One, "Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit").

## Mitigations
- Stack canaries: a random value placed between locals and the return address; checked before return; mismatch aborts (gcc -fstack-protector). Defeated by leaks or by overwrites that skip the canary.
- NX/DEP (W^X): stack and heap pages are non-executable, so injected shellcode will not run.
- ASLR: randomize stack, heap, library and executable (PIE) base addresses so the attacker cannot hardcode targets.
- Return-oriented programming (ROP) bypasses NX by chaining existing code snippets ("gadgets") ending in ret; CFI and shadow stacks (Intel CET) counter it.
- Fortify source, bounds-checked functions, compiler warnings, sanitizers (ASan) in testing, fuzzing.
- Memory-safe languages (Rust, Go, Java) eliminate most of this class; roughly two-thirds or more of severe vulnerabilities in large C/C++ codebases have been reported as memory safety issues by Microsoft and Google, which is why they are moving to safe languages.

## Related bug classes
- Heap overflow (corrupt allocator metadata or adjacent objects), use-after-free, format-string bugs (printf(user_input)), integer overflow leading to a small allocation.
- Heartbleed (2014): a missing bounds check on a read (buffer over-read), leaking memory.

## Fixes at code level
Use length-aware APIs (strncpy with care, snprintf, strlcpy, std::string, span), validate lengths before copying, compile with hardening flags.

## Follow-ups
- Why does ASLR need an info leak to be defeated? The attacker needs one known address to compute the others.
- Why not just make the stack non-executable? ROP and data-only attacks still work.
keyPoints: Overflowing a stack buffer can overwrite the saved return address and redirect execution.
Defenses stack up: canaries, NX/DEP, ASLR, CFI/shadow stacks; each can be bypassed alone (leaks, ROP).
Use bounds-checked APIs or memory-safe languages and test with sanitizers and fuzzers.
Heap overflows, use-after-free and format-string bugs are siblings of the stack overflow.

os-security-basics:3.body:
## Two ways to isolate workloads
Virtual machine: a hypervisor emulates hardware; each VM runs its own full guest kernel and OS. Container: a normal process (or group) on the host kernel, isolated using kernel features.

## Container isolation building blocks (Linux)
- Namespaces: give a process its own view of PIDs, mount points, network, hostname, users (user namespace maps uid 0 inside to an unprivileged uid outside), IPC, cgroup.
- cgroups: limit and account CPU, memory, I/O, pids; memory limit exceeded triggers the OOM killer inside the cgroup.
- Capabilities, seccomp-bpf syscall filters (Docker's default profile blocks around 40-50 syscalls), AppArmor/SELinux profiles, read-only root filesystems.

## VM isolation
- Hypervisor (KVM, Xen, Hyper-V, ESXi) uses hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V, nested page tables). Guest kernels are separate; the attack surface is the hypervisor and device emulation, which is much smaller than the whole syscall interface of a shared kernel.
- Lightweight VMs combine both: AWS Firecracker (used by Lambda and Fargate) boots a microVM in around 125 ms with a minimal device model; Kata Containers and gVisor (a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls) add stronger isolation for containers.

## Comparison
- Startup: containers in milliseconds to a second; VMs in seconds (microVMs ~100+ ms).
- Overhead: containers near zero memory beyond the app; a VM carries a guest OS (hundreds of MB).
- Density: hundreds of containers per host versus tens of VMs.
- Isolation: VMs stronger (separate kernel); a kernel vulnerability or misconfiguration (privileged container, mounting docker.sock, host PID namespace) can let a container escape to the host.
- OS flexibility: a container shares the host kernel (Linux containers need a Linux kernel); a VM can run any OS.

## When to use what
- Trusted workloads from one team, fast scaling: containers.
- Multi-tenant, running untrusted code (serverless, CI for strangers, SaaS sandboxes): VMs, microVMs or gVisor, ideally with containers inside.
- Defense in depth: containers inside VMs is the usual cloud pattern; Kubernetes nodes are VMs.

## Hardening checklist for containers
Run as non-root, drop all capabilities then add only needed, read-only filesystem, default seccomp profile, no privileged mode, resource limits, patched host kernel, minimal base images.

## Follow-ups
- Is a container a VM? No: no separate kernel.
- Why are Lambda functions in microVMs rather than plain containers? Strong tenant isolation with fast startup.
keyPoints: Containers share the host kernel and use namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and seccomp; VMs have their own kernel behind a hypervisor.
VMs offer stronger isolation, containers offer faster starts and higher density.
Untrusted multi-tenant code warrants VMs, microVMs (Firecracker) or gVisor.
Privileged containers and exposed docker.sock defeat container isolation.

os-security-basics:4.body:
## Principle
Every program, user and component should have only the minimum privileges needed to do its job, for the minimum time. When something is compromised or buggy, the damage is limited to what it could do.

## At the OS level
- Do not run services as root. Create a dedicated unprivileged user per service.
- Capabilities instead of root: a web server needing port 80 gets CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE only (or binds high port behind a proxy).
- Privilege separation: OpenSSH splits into a privileged monitor and an unprivileged child that handles untrusted network input; Chrome splits the sandboxed renderer from the browser process.
- Drop privileges after startup: bind the port as root, then setuid to an unprivileged user (nginx master vs workers).
- seccomp filters to block syscalls the program never needs; AppArmor/SELinux policy; read-only filesystems; separate namespaces.
- setuid binaries: keep them minimal; prefer sudoers rules naming exact commands over blanket access.
- File permissions: 0600 for secrets, not 0644; umask defaults.

## In cloud and applications
- IAM: grant narrowly scoped policies (s3:GetObject on one bucket prefix, not s3:*), short-lived credentials (role assumption, STS tokens), separate roles per service.
- Database accounts: the app user gets SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on specific tables, not DDL or superuser; separate migration and read-only reporting users.
- Kubernetes: ServiceAccounts with narrow RBAC, no cluster-admin for apps, NetworkPolicies, PodSecurity standards.
- Secrets: scoped per service, rotated, never in images or repos.

## Worked example
A image-resizing service reads from bucket in and writes to bucket out. Policy: GetObject on in/*, PutObject on out/*. An SSRF or RCE bug in the resizer now cannot read customer database backups or delete data. With a broad s3:* policy the same bug is a data breach.

## Trade-offs
- More operational work: policy authoring, debugging denials, access request flows.
- Too tight breaks features; start with audit or permissive mode, observe actual usage (e.g. IAM Access Analyzer, strace, audit logs), then tighten.
- Complements, not replaces, input validation and patching: it limits blast radius.

## Related ideas
Defense in depth, separation of duties, default deny, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975).

## Follow-ups
- Why is running as root in a container risky even with namespaces? A kernel or runtime bug can map to real root on the host unless user namespaces are used.
- Time-bound privilege: just-in-time access, expiring tokens.
keyPoints: Grant the minimum privileges for the minimum time so that a compromise has a small blast radius.
Run services as unprivileged users, use capabilities, drop privileges after startup and separate privileged from untrusted-input code.
In cloud IAM and databases, scope policies to specific actions and resources and prefer short-lived credentials.
Tighten gradually by observing real usage; it complements patching and validation.

os-security-basics:5.body:
## What TOCTOU is
Time-of-check to time-of-use: a program checks a property of a resource, then acts on it, but the resource can change in between. The check result is stale at the time of use. It is a race condition, and the attacker's goal is to win the window.

## Classic file example
```c
if (access("/tmp/report", W_OK) == 0) {     // check as the real user
    fd = open("/tmp/report", O_WRONLY);     // use as setuid root
    write(fd, data, n);
}
```
A setuid program checks that the real user may write to /tmp/report, then opens it. In between, the attacker replaces /tmp/report with a symlink to /etc/passwd. open follows the symlink with root privileges and the attacker overwrites a protected file. Window: microseconds, but an attacker can retry thousands of times (and can widen it by slowing the target, for example by making the kernel evict path lookups or by filling CPU).

## Fixes
- Do not check; just try, and handle failure. Use the identity of the actor at the operation: drop privileges (seteuid) before open so the kernel does the check atomically with the use.
- Operate on file descriptors, not names: open once, then fstat/fchmod/fchown on the fd (the fd refers to the same inode regardless of path changes).
- Use atomic flags: open(path, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW) so creation fails if the file exists or is a symlink; mkstemp for temp files in secure directories instead of predictable names in /tmp.
- openat with directory fds, and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS (openat2) to constrain resolution; sticky bit on /tmp (protected_symlinks, protected_regular sysctls).
- Atomic rename for updates (write temp, fsync, rename).

## Not only files
- Check-then-act on application state: if balance >= x then debit (see async races); fix with atomic conditional updates or transactions.
- Web: coupon redeemed twice with parallel requests (limit-overrun race); fix with unique constraints or atomic decrements. Single-packet attack techniques fire dozens of requests in the same TCP packet to hit the window.
- Kernel/user: a syscall validates a user buffer and then reads it again, while another thread changes it between (double fetch). Fix by copying once into kernel memory before validating.
- Cloud: check an S3 object's content then process the object after it was overwritten; use versions or ETags.
- Time-of-check in permission systems: token validated at connection start and revoked later.

## Interview framing
Name the window, the attacker control (symlink swap, parallel request, other thread) and make the check and the use one atomic step (atomic syscall flags, transactions, constraints, locks on the same resource), or bind to a stable handle (fd, inode, row id).

## Follow-ups
- Why does stat-then-open fail where open-then-fstat works? The first identifies by name twice, the second identifies the object once.
- Is locking the answer? Only if every party (including the attacker's path) honors the lock; advisory locks do not stop an attacker.
keyPoints: TOCTOU is a race between checking a condition and using the result; the attacker changes the resource in the gap.
Classic case: access() then open() on a path swapped for a symlink; fix by acting on a file descriptor or using O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW and dropping privileges.
The same pattern appears as double-spend and limit-overrun races in web apps; fix with atomic DB operations or unique constraints.
Make check and use a single atomic step or bind to a stable handle.
